title: Accuracy under a prevalence shift
body: A fixed binary classifier has sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.90. What is its accuracy when the positive-class prevalence is 0.10? What is it when the prevalence is 0.50, assuming the class-specific rates stay fixed? Explain why the two accuracies differ.
answer: With prevalence π, accuracy = π·sensitivity + (1−π)·specificity. At prevalence 0.10 it is 0.10(0.80)+0.90(0.90)=0.89. At prevalence 0.50 it is 0.50(0.80)+0.50(0.90)=0.85. The classifier's conditional error rates are unchanged, but overall accuracy weights them by the class mix, which has changed.

title: Completeness and an unbiased pair probability
body: In three independent Bernoulli trials let T be the success count. Show that h(T)=T(T-1)/6 is unbiased for p², and evaluate it at T=2. Why is this function unique among unbiased functions of T when p ranges over (0,1)?
answer: There are six ordered pairs of distinct trials. Each pair succeeds with probability p², so E[T(T-1)/6]=p². At T=2 the estimate is 2/6=1/3. If another function of T were unbiased for p², its difference from h would have expectation zero for every p. The binomial count is complete on (0,1), so the difference is zero almost surely.

title: A sufficient count that is not complete
body: Let T count successes in two independent Bernoulli trials, but suppose the model permits only p=1/2. Find a nonzero function q(T) whose expectation is zero, and explain what changes if p can range through (0,1).
answer: Take q(T)=T-1. At the sole allowed value p=1/2, E[T]=2p=1, so E[q(T)]=0, although q(T) is -1 or 1 with positive probability. Thus T is not complete for the restricted model. If p varies through (0,1), E[q(T)]=2p-1 is not identically zero; indeed the binomial polynomial argument shows no nonzero q has zero expectation for every p in that interval.

title: A highest-posterior-probability set on a grid
body: A parameter can take values 1, 2 and 3 with posterior probabilities 0.50, 0.30 and 0.20. Give a smallest set with posterior probability at least 80%, choosing the most probable points first. Why does a continuous-density threshold formula need care here?
answer: The set {1,2} has posterior probability 0.50+0.30=0.80 and uses two points; no one-point set reaches 0.80. In a discrete distribution probability arrives in jumps, so an exact target may be unattainable at some levels and a threshold may include tied points. Specify at-least content and a rule for ties or excess mass.

title: Which measurements can the events distinguish?
body: Let Ω={a,b,c,d} and F={∅,{a,b},{c,d},Ω}. Is X with values (2,2,3,3) measurable? Is Y with values (0,1,0,1) measurable? Exhibit a threshold event for each answer.
answer: X is measurable: for 2≤t<3, {X≤t}={a,b}, with ∅ below 2 and Ω at or above 3. All are in F. Y is not measurable: for 0≤t<1, {Y≤t}={a,c}, which is not in F. The same four numerical outcomes can support one measurement but not the other because F distinguishes only the two blocks.

title: A transformed uniform measurement
body: On Ω=(0,1) with Borel events and uniform probability, let $X(\omega)=\omega$ and $W=X^2$. Explain why $W$ is measurable, then compute $P(W\le 1/4)$ and $P(1/4<W\le 9/16)$.
answer: The square function is continuous, hence Borel measurable; its composition with X is measurable. Since ω is positive, {W≤1/4}=(0,1/2], whose probability is 1/2. Also {1/4<W≤9/16}=(1/2,3/4], whose probability is 3/4−1/2=1/4. These are probabilities of inverse-image events, not areas under a guessed density.

title: Uncertainty beyond a conditional shrinkage rule
body: A hierarchical analysis assigns equal posterior probability to two hyperparameter regimes. In regime A a group effect has conditional posterior N(5,1), and in regime B it has conditional posterior N(9,1). Find the marginal posterior mean and variance of the group effect. What variance term would a calculation based on only one regime omit?
answer: The marginal mean is $(5+9)/2=7$. The law of total variance gives $E[\mathrm{Var}(\theta\mid\mathrm{regime},y)]+\mathrm{Var}(E[\theta\mid\mathrm{regime},y])=1+[(5-7)^2+(9-7)^2]/2=1+4=5$. Fixing a single regime would retain only conditional variance 1 and omit the between-regime variance 4. This is the distinction between a conditional shrinkage calculation and full averaging over uncertain hyperparameters.

title: A percentile between observations
body: The ordered sample is 1, 3, 5, 9, 12. Find its p=0.6 quantile by (a) the empirical-CDF inverse and (b) R's type-7 interpolation rule. Explain why they differ.
answer: The empirical inverse uses index ceil(5×0.6)=3 and gives x_(3)=5. Type 7 uses h=1+(5−1)×0.6=3.4, so it interpolates 40% from x_(3)=5 to x_(4)=9, giving 5+0.4(9−5)=6.6. The empirical CDF is a step function, whereas type 7 fills the gap between adjacent order statistics.

title: A quartile with tied observations
body: The ordered sample is 2, 2, 2, 9. Find the 0.75 quantile by the empirical-CDF inverse and by R's type-7 rule. What does the difference show?
answer: The empirical inverse uses ceil(4×0.75)=3 and returns x_(3)=2: three of four values are already at most 2. Type 7 uses h=1+3×0.75=3.25 and returns 2+0.25(9−2)=3.75. Interpolation can put a reported quantile where no value was observed, especially when a large CDF jump from ties sits beside a gap.

title: Exchangeable but dependent draws
body: A bag has one red and one blue ball. Draw both without replacement, marking red as 1. Give the probabilities of (1,0) and (0,1). Are the draws exchangeable? Are they independent?
answer: The two ordered outcomes each have probability 1/2, so permuting draw positions preserves the joint law: the pair is exchangeable. Each marginal probability of red is 1/2, but P(1,1)=0 rather than (1/2)(1/2)=1/4, so the draws are dependent. Their covariance is -1/4.

title: A smooth and its intercept
body: At three observed inputs a fitted additive predictor has intercept 2 and smooth values (-1, 0, 1). Give its three fitted predictors. If the intercept is changed to 5, choose smooth values that give the same predictors. State one constraint that picks a unique intercept in this example.
answer: The fitted predictors are (1, 2, 3). Raising the intercept by 3 and lowering every smooth value by 3 gives intercept 5 and smooth values (-4, -3, -2), with the same predictors. The sum-to-zero constraint on the smooth selects the original values, whose sum is 0; the shifted smooth sums to -9.

title: Only a product is visible
body: A binary response has success probability p=ab, where 0<a<1 and 0<b<1. Compare (a,b)=(0.2,0.5) with (0.5,0.2). Are a and b separately identifiable from any number of these binary responses? Is their product identifiable?
answer: Both pairs give p=0.1, so each generates the same Bernoulli law for every response and every sample size. The individual factors a and b are not identified. The product ab is identified because distinct products give distinct Bernoulli success probabilities.

title: One category from a Dirichlet vector
body: A three-category probability vector has a Dirichlet(1,2,3) prior. What is the marginal distribution and variance of the first probability? What is its covariance with the second probability?
answer: The first coordinate is Beta(1,5). Its variance is 1·5/[6²(6+1)]=5/252≈0.01984. The covariance of the first and second coordinates is -1·2/[6²(6+1)]=-1/126≈-0.00794. The negative covariance reflects that the shares must sum to one.

title: A new category after counts
body: Start with Dirichlet(1,1,1) probabilities and observe category counts (2,0,1). What is the posterior vector of concentrations, and what is the posterior predictive probability that the next observation is in category 2?
answer: Adding the counts gives Dirichlet(3,1,2), total concentration 6. Integrating the category-2 probability over this posterior gives its posterior mean 1/6≈0.1667. The zero observed count does not make its predictive probability zero.

title: A shared coin probability
body: Choose a coin probability Θ to be 0.2 or 0.8 with equal probability, then toss twice independently conditional on Θ. Are the two results exchangeable? Are they independent after Θ is integrated out? Calculate P(1,0) and P(1,1).
answer: The conditional iid construction makes the joint law exchangeable. P(1,0)=0.5(0.2·0.8)+0.5(0.8·0.2)=0.16, while P(1,1)=0.5(0.2²)+0.5(0.8²)=0.34. Each marginal success probability is 0.5, so independence would require P(1,1)=0.25. The shared random Θ creates dependence.

title: A density bar taller than one
body: Ten observations fall in two adjacent bins. Six are in $[0,0.2)$ and four are in $[0.2,1)$. Find the heights and areas of a density histogram. Is a bar height greater than one an error?
answer: The widths are $0.2$ and $0.8$. The density heights are $6/(10\cdot0.2)=3$ and $4/(10\cdot0.8)=0.5$. The areas are $3\cdot0.2=0.6$ and $0.5\cdot0.8=0.4$, summing to one. Height $3$ is valid: density is probability per unit of the horizontal scale, while each bar's area is its probability share.

title: Shifting histogram boundaries
body: The measurements are $0.4,0.6,1.4,1.6,2.4$. Count them first in $[0,1),[1,2),[2,3)$, then in $[-0.5,0.5),[0.5,1.5),[1.5,2.5)$. What changes, and what should that tell you about interpreting a peak from five values?
answer: The first grid has counts $(2,2,1)$. The shifted grid has counts $(1,2,2)$. The data have not changed: one measurement moves from the first bar to the second, and another from the second to the third because the boundaries moved. A peak or asymmetry inferred from five binned observations is sensitive to that choice; inspect the raw values and several reasonable grids.

title: A boundary left by an improper prior
body: A binomial success probability has prior weight $w(\theta)\propto[\theta(1-\theta)]^{-1}$. For five trials, determine the posterior kernel and whether it is proper (a) if two trials succeed and (b) if none succeed. Give the posterior mean in the proper case.
answer: For two successes, the kernel is $\theta^{2-1}(1-\theta)^{3-1}$, hence the proper $\operatorname{Beta}(2,3)$ posterior has mean $2/(2+3)=0.4$. With no successes, the kernel is $\theta^{-1}(1-\theta)^4$; its integral diverges at zero, so there is no posterior probability distribution.

title: A boxplot flag is a question
body: The ordered observations are $1,2,3,3,4,5,6,7,16$. Using hinges that include the median in both halves, find the $1.5IQR$ fences and identify any flagged value. The record confirms that the flagged value was measured correctly. Should it be deleted solely because of the fence?
answer: The median is $4$. The lower and upper hinges are $3$ and $6$, so $IQR=3$. The fences are $3-1.5(3)=-1.5$ and $6+1.5(3)=10.5$. Only $16$ is flagged. The fence signals an observation worth investigating; a confirmed genuine measurement should not be silently deleted. Report a sensitivity analysis or fit a model suitable for the tail if its influence matters.

title: A distant point with a modest z-score
body: For the observations $0,0,0,24$, compute the mean, the usual sample standard deviation, and the z-score of $24$. Would a rule requiring absolute z-score above $2$ flag it? Explain the self-masking effect.
answer: The mean is $6$. The squared deviations sum to $432$, so the sample variance is $432/3=144$ and the sample standard deviation is $12$. The score of $24$ is $(24-6)/12=1.5$, below $2$. The distant point also raises the mean and standard deviation used to judge itself. For $n=4$, the sharp upper bound on any ordinary sample z-score is $(n-1)/\sqrt n=3/2=1.5$.

title: A cluster sandwich calculation
body: An intercept-only model has three independent clusters, each with two observations: $(1,2)$, $(3,4)$ and $(5,6)$. Compute the fitted mean, the bread $A$, the sum of squared cluster residual totals $B$, and the uncorrected sandwich variance $A^{-1}BA^{-1}$. Why should the usual large-cluster normal approximation be treated cautiously?
answer: The fitted mean is $3.5$. Cluster residual totals are $-4,0,4$, so $A=6$ and $B=16+0+16=32$. The variance is $32/36\approx0.8889$. With only three independent clusters the asymptotic normal approximation for inference can be poor.

title: Population-average risk contrast
body: Four control patients each have two binary outcomes, (0,0), (0,0), (1,1), (0,0). Four treated patients have (1,1), (1,1), (0,0), (1,1). Calculate the observed marginal risks, risk difference, and odds ratio. How many independent patients, rather than visits, contribute?
answer: There are 2 control events in 8 visits and 6 treated events in 8 visits, so the marginal risks are 1/4 and 3/4 and the risk difference is 1/2. Their odds are 1/3 and 3, giving odds ratio 9. There are 8 independent patient clusters, four per group, even though there are 16 visits.

title: Can binary margins correlate perfectly?
body: Binary variables A and B have success probabilities 0.2 and 0.8. What is the largest possible value of $P(A=1,B=1)$? Use it to find their maximum possible covariance and correlation. Explain why a proposed correlation of 0.6 cannot describe a true joint Bernoulli law with these margins.
answer: The joint success probability cannot exceed min(0.2,0.8)=0.2. The maximum covariance is 0.2-(0.2)(0.8)=0.04. Both variances equal 0.16, so their standard-deviation product is 0.16 and the maximum correlation is 0.04/0.16=0.25. A correlation of 0.6 exceeds that bound and cannot arise from these margins.

title: Working correlation and mean validity
body: An analyst models a repeated binary outcome's marginal mean correctly but uses an independence working correlation when within-person responses are positively associated. Another analyst uses an exchangeable working correlation but omits an important mean covariate. Which analyst has the usual GEE consistency argument for the target mean coefficient, and what role does a sandwich covariance play? State the sampling condition that matters.
answer: The first analyst retains the usual consistency argument: with many independent clusters, regularity and suitable missingness, a correct mean makes the GEE score unbiased even if the working association is wrong. A cluster sandwich covariance estimates the resulting coefficient uncertainty. The second analyst's correct-looking working correlation does not repair an omitted mean covariate; a sandwich only changes uncertainty around the fitted estimating equation. Few or dependent clusters undermine the large-sample argument.

title: A curve hidden by correlation
body: Five paired values have $x=(-2,-1,0,1,2)$ and $y=(4,1,0,1,4)$. What does their scatterplot show? Compute the centered cross-product sum and say whether zero correlation would imply no relationship here.
answer: The points lie exactly on the parabola $y=x^2$. The means are $\bar x=0$ and $\bar y=2$, so the cross-product sum is $-4+1+0-1+4=0$ and the sample correlation is zero. The relationship is exact but nonlinear; zero correlation rules out a linear trend in these five points, not a relationship.

title: Repeated pairs on a scatterplot
body: A plot of rounded height and weight contains a dot at one coordinate. Twenty people may have that same recorded pair. What can the dot tell you, what can it not tell you, and how could you show the multiplicity without changing the measurements used in analysis?
answer: The dot shows at least one observed pair at that coordinate, but a conventional point plot does not reveal whether one or twenty observations overlap there. Transparency, a count-sized symbol, or small display-only jitter can show the pile. The original recorded pairs, not the jittered drawing positions, remain the data for a correlation or regression.

title: Equal moments with changing laws
body: Let independent $X_t$ be $-1$ or $1$ equally likely at even times, and let it be $0$ with probability $1/2$ and each of $-\sqrt2,\sqrt2$ with probability $1/4$ at odd times. Compute the mean, variance and nonzero-lag covariance. Is the process weakly stationary? Is it strictly stationary? Explain.
answer: At either parity the mean is $0$. The even-time variance is $1$; the odd-time variance is $(1/4)2+(1/4)2=1$. Independence makes covariance $0$ at every nonzero lag. Thus the mean and lag covariance are time invariant and the process is weakly stationary. Its one-time law alternates between a two-point and a three-point distribution, so it is not strictly stationary.

title: What does the placebo contrast estimate?
body: In a randomized masked trial, 45 of 60 people assigned active treatment improve, compared with 30 of 60 assigned a matching placebo. Compute the two improvement proportions and the active-minus-placebo risk difference. Does the placebo group's improvement rate equal a pure expectancy effect?
answer: The proportions are 45/60=0.75 and 30/60=0.50, so the risk difference is 0.25 or 25 percentage points. The placebo improvement rate includes natural recovery, measurement fluctuation, shared care and any expectancy influence; it does not isolate expectancy.

title: Concealment and masking at different times
body: A recruiter can see the next assignment before enrolling a participant, but participants and outcome assessors are masked after enrolment. Which design protection is missing? Give one route by which it could bias the comparison, and state whether masking afterward repairs it.
answer: Allocation concealment is missing. A recruiter could preferentially enroll a sicker or healthier participant when the next assignment is known, producing baseline imbalance related to treatment. Later masking cannot undo that selection, although it can limit post-assignment behaviour and measurement biases.

title: A sample size from Chebyshev's bound
body: Independent observations have population variance 25. How many are needed so that Chebyshev's inequality guarantees P(|sample mean - population mean|≥1)≤0.05? State why the calculation could fail for correlated observations.
answer: For n independent observations, Var(sample mean)=25/n and Chebyshev bounds the probability by 25/n. Requiring 25/n≤0.05 gives n≥500. Correlation changes the variance of the average, so the 25/n formula may fail.

title: A class mean with partial pooling
body: For a normal hierarchy with known population mean μ=40, between-class variance τ²=9 and within-class variance σ²=36, a class of four has sample mean 55. Find its conditional posterior weight on its own mean, posterior mean and posterior variance.
answer: The weight is nτ²/(σ²+nτ²)=4(9)/(36+4(9))=1/2. The posterior mean is (1/2)55+(1/2)40=47.5. The variance is σ²τ²/(σ²+nτ²)=36(9)/72=4.5. This is conditional on the supplied population parameters.

title: Conditional independence can hide marginal dependence
body: Let θ be uniform on [0,1], and conditionally on θ let Y₁ and Y₂ be independent Bernoulli(θ). Find P(Y₁=1), P(Y₁=1,Y₂=1), and Cov(Y₁,Y₂). Are the two observations marginally independent?
answer: Eθ=1/2, so P(Y₁=1)=1/2. Conditional independence gives P(Y₁=1,Y₂=1)=Eθ²=1/3. Thus Cov(Y₁,Y₂)=1/3-(1/2)²=1/12>0. Sharing an uncertain θ makes them marginally dependent.

title: Does this reference posterior exist?
body: For a Gaussian linear model with the reference measure π(β,σ²)∝1/σ², consider (a) n=5, p=2, full-rank X and residual sum of squares 6; (b) the same n and p but a rank-one X; (c) full-rank X but residual sum of squares zero. In which cases is the posterior proper, and why?
answer: Only (a) is proper: n-p=3>0 and the positive residual sum of squares controls the variance integral. In (b), a coefficient direction is unidentified and the flat prior leaves infinite mass. In (c), the variance kernel diverges near zero.

title: A reference posterior from three observations
body: In an intercept-only normal model, observations are 1, 2 and 3. Under π(β,σ²)∝1/σ², find the fitted mean, residual sum of squares, residual degrees of freedom and inverse-Gamma posterior parameters for σ².
answer: The fitted mean is 2 and the squared residuals are 1, 0 and 1, summing to 2. With n=3 and p=1, the residual degrees of freedom are 2. Hence σ² given the data is inverse-Gamma with shape (n-p)/2=1 and scale SSE/2=1. It is proper, but its mean is infinite.

title: A Bernoulli sum through its MGF
body: Let X and Y be independent Bernoulli variables with success probability 0.4. Find the MGF of $S=X+Y$, its mean and variance, and $P(S=2)$. What part fails if $X=Y$ instead?
answer: One MGF is $0.6+0.4e^{t}$, so independence gives $M_S(t)=(0.6+0.4e^{t})^{2}$. The mean is $0.8$, variance $2(0.4)(0.6)=0.48$, and $P(S=2)=0.4^{2}=0.16$. If $X=Y$, the sum's MGF is $0.6+0.4e^{2t}$; the product rule and binomial law do not apply.

title: An exponential transform's domain
body: For $X$ exponential with rate 3, derive $M_X(t)$, give its domain, then calculate $E(X)$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ and $M_X(2)$. Why is substituting t=4 into the rational expression invalid as an MGF calculation?
answer: Integrating $3e^{-(3-t)x}$ over $x\ge 0$ gives $M_X(t)=3/(3-t)$ for $t<3$. Thus $E(X)=1/3$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=1/9$, and $M_X(2)=3$. At t=4 the defining integral diverges; the algebraic value -3 is not an expectation.

title: An autoregression two steps ahead
body: A stationary AR(1) series has mean 20, coefficient 0.6, innovation variance 9, and latest value 30. Find the conditional-mean forecasts one and two steps ahead and the corresponding forecast-error variances.
answer: The forecasts are 20+0.6(30-20)=26 and 20+0.6²(30-20)=23.6. The error variances are 9 and 9(1+0.6²)=12.24. The second forecast has moved toward the mean while uncertainty has increased.

title: Which forecast is best under each loss?
body: Conditional on today's information, tomorrow's demand is 10 with probability 0.8 and 30 with probability 0.2. Give a forecast minimizing squared error and one minimizing absolute error. Explain why they differ.
answer: The conditional mean is 0.8(10)+0.2(30)=14, which minimizes squared error. The conditional median is 10, which minimizes absolute error because 80% of the conditional probability lies there. The two losses penalize misses differently.

title: A nonunique posterior median
body: A posterior puts probability 0.5 on θ=1 and 0.5 on θ=5. Which actions minimize posterior expected absolute error, and which action minimizes squared error? Give both risks at action 2.
answer: Every action in [1,5] is a posterior median and has absolute-error risk 0.5|a-1|+0.5|a-5|=2, including a=2. The posterior mean 3 uniquely minimizes squared error. At a=2 the squared-error risk is 0.5(1²)+0.5(3²)=5.

title: Transforming a posterior median
body: A probability θ has a posterior median 0.25. What is the posterior median of its odds θ/(1-θ)? Explain whether the odds of the posterior mean must equal the posterior mean of the odds.
answer: Odds are a strictly increasing function of θ, so their median is 0.25/(1-0.25)=1/3. Means do not generally commute with nonlinear transformations: E[θ/(1-θ)|x] need not equal E[θ|x]/(1-E[θ|x]), and the former may not even exist for some posteriors.

title: Interpret a fitted probit dose curve
body: A binary probit model is p(x)=Φ(-1+0.5x). Find p at x=0, 2 and 4, the dose where p=0.5, and the local probability derivative at that dose. Explain why the coefficient is not a probability increase.
answer: The normal scores are -1, 0 and 1, giving p≈0.15866, 0.5 and 0.84134. The half-probability dose is x=2. The derivative there is 0.5φ(0)=0.5/√(2π)≈0.19947 per unit of x; elsewhere the derivative is 0.5φ(-1+0.5x), so it is not constant.

title: A return without staying put
body: A two-state chain has P(A→A)=0.7, P(A→B)=0.3, P(B→A)=0.4 and P(B→B)=0.6. Is A recurrent even though it may leave immediately? Find its expected first return time from A.
answer: The finite chain is irreducible, so both states are positive recurrent. From B the geometric waiting time to hit A has mean 1/0.4=2.5. Starting A, return time is 1 with probability 0.7; otherwise it is 1 plus that waiting time. Its mean is 0.7(1)+0.3(1+2.5)=1.75. Leaving immediately does not prevent eventual return.

title: A binomial count below Poisson variance
body: A count is binomial with five trials and success probability 0.4. Find its mean, variance and variance-to-mean ratio. Compare its variance with a Poisson count having the same mean.
answer: The mean is 5(0.4)=2 and the variance is 5(0.4)(0.6)=1.2. Its variance-to-mean ratio is 1.2/2=0.6. A Poisson count with mean 2 has variance 2, so this binomial mechanism is underdispersed relative to that Poisson reference.

title: Conditional spread versus pooled spread
body: Five units in group A each have count 1; five in group B each have count 5. Compute the pooled sample mean and variance, then describe the within-group variance. Why can a pooled mean–variance comparison misdiagnose dispersion?
answer: The pooled mean is 3 and the pooled sample variance is 40/9≈4.444, greater than the pooled mean. Within each group the sample variance is zero. The group indicator explains the mean shift; dispersion should be assessed conditional on fitted group means rather than from the pooled counts.

title: Autocovariances of a stationary AR(1)
body: A stationary AR(1) has coefficient $0.4$ and independent innovation variance $9$. Find its variance $\gamma(0)$, lag-one autocovariance $\gamma(1)$ and lag-two autocorrelation $\rho(2)$.
answer: Stationarity gives $\gamma(0)=0.4^2\gamma(0)+9$, so $\gamma(0)=75/7\approx10.7143$. Then $\gamma(1)=0.4\gamma(0)=30/7\approx4.2857$, while $\rho(2)=0.4^2=0.16$. These quantities depend on lag, not on the calendar origin.

title: Stable moments, changing distributions
body: All variables in a time series are independent. Even-time values equal $-1$ or $1$ with equal probabilities; odd-time values are uniform on $[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3]$. Is the series weakly stationary? Is it strictly stationary? Explain using means, variances, covariances and one-time distributions.
answer: Both marginal laws have mean $0$ and variance $1$; independence makes every covariance at a nonzero lag equal to $0$. Thus the process is weakly stationary. The even-time law has two atoms and the odd-time law is continuous, so shifting by one time step changes a marginal distribution and strict stationarity fails.

title: Binary GLM likelihood contribution
body: Two conditionally independent binary outcomes are y=(0,1), with fitted event probabilities p=(0.25,0.60). What is their joint likelihood contribution?
answer: The zero contributes 1-0.25=0.75 and the one contributes 0.60. Conditional independence gives 0.75*0.60=0.45.

title: Bernoulli mean and variance
body: A binary GLM predicts event probability 0.8 for a patient. Give the conditional mean and variance of that patient's zero-one response, and explain why its variance is not 0.8.
answer: The mean is p=0.8 and variance is p(1-p)=0.8*0.2=0.16. Bernoulli variance accounts for both possible outcomes and is largest at p=0.5.

title: Changing a binary GLM link
body: If a logit and probit model both assign probability p=0.4 to an observed event, do they give different Bernoulli likelihood contributions for that observation? What does the link change?
answer: No; each gives likelihood contribution 0.4 for an observed one. The link changes how the predictors map to the probability and therefore can change fitted probabilities and coefficient meanings, while the Bernoulli mass at a given p is unchanged.

title: A fitted cholesterol probability
body: The displayed logistic model has score -9.3203-0.1094 I(male)+1.5842 cholesterol. Find the fitted disease probability for a male at cholesterol 5.5 and compare with a female at the same value.
answer: The male score is -0.7166 and the inverse-logit probability is about 0.32814. The female score is -0.6072 and probability about 0.35270. Their conditional probability difference is about -0.02456; this does not determine the marginal sex difference.

title: Odds and causation in the cholesterol example
body: The fitted cholesterol slope is 1.5842. Explain what exp(1.5842) compares and why it does not prove that an intervention lowering cholesterol would change disease risk.
answer: At the same sex, a one-unit higher cholesterol value has fitted disease odds exp(1.5842), about 4.88 times as large. The data description does not establish random assignment, control all confounders or document a causal intervention; the coefficient is an adjusted association in the fitted model.

title: Complementary log-log probability update
body: A complementary log-log model has baseline event probability 0.20. A one-unit covariate change has coefficient log(2). Find the new event probability and state which quantity doubles.
answer: Write $H=-\log(1-p)$. Initially $H=-\log(0.8)$. The coefficient doubles $H$, so $1-p_{\mathrm{new}}=\exp(-2H)=0.8^2=0.64$ and $p_{\mathrm{new}}=0.36$. The negative log of the no-event probability doubles; the event probability does not.

title: Reading a complementary log-log coefficient
body: In a binary cloglog regression, a coefficient is log(3). What exactly is multiplied by three, and when can it be called a hazard ratio?
answer: The quantity -log(1-p), where p is the fitted event probability, is multiplied by three. A hazard-ratio interpretation additionally requires a suitable proportional-hazards model for event times; an arbitrary cross-sectional binary response does not supply that interpretation. Neither the odds nor probability generally triples.

title: Reversing the event in a cloglog model
body: A fitted complementary log-log model describes event probability p. Does negating its coefficients give the same-link model for the nonevent probability 1-p? Explain.
answer: No. The inverse cloglog curve is asymmetric, so reversing the outcome changes the link to its log-log counterpart; simple coefficient sign reversal is the logit's symmetry. Refit or transform the model explicitly for the chosen event definition.

title: Which parameter supplies E-step weights?
body: In Q(Psi;Psi_old), which argument determines the conditional distribution of the missing labels, and which is optimized in the M step?
answer: Psi_old fixes the conditional distribution and therefore all E-step responsibilities. The candidate Psi is varied in the M step while those responsibilities stay fixed.

title: Equal component densities
body: Two mixture components have equal density at x, but current weights 0.8 and 0.2. Find the E-step responsibility of the first component.
answer: It is 0.8: Bayes' numerator multiplies each density by its current mixture weight, and the equal densities cancel.

title: A symmetric normal-mixture E step
body: Two unit-variance normal components have equal current weights and means 0 and 2. Find the responsibility for the first component at x=1.
answer: Both weighted densities agree at the midpoint, so the responsibility is 1/2. This is conditional uncertainty, not an observed class label.

title: Correlation in an ensemble average
body: Four numerical predictors have error variance 1 each and pairwise correlation 0.5. Find the variance of their average under this equal-correlation model.
answer: It is 0.5+(1-0.5)/4=0.625. The independent case would give 0.25; common error does not disappear as the ensemble grows.

title: Voting is not averaging labels
body: Three classifiers predict category labels A, A and B. What is the plurality result, and why does the numerical squared-error identity for a mean not prove anything about this vote?
answer: A wins with two votes. Category names are not numerical values, and zero-one classification loss after a vote is not squared loss of an average.

title: How members differ
body: Contrast the mechanism making members different in bagging, a random forest, and AdaBoost.
answer: Bagging fits the base learner to bootstrap resamples. A random forest adds random candidate-variable choices at tree splits. AdaBoost sequentially changes training-example weights to emphasize difficult cases and combines weighted learners.

title: Two directions of Jensen's inequality
body: Let X equal 1 or 4, each with probability one half. Compare $E(X^2)$ with $(EX)^2$ and $E(\log X)$ with $\log(EX)$. Explain the opposite directions.
answer: $EX=2.5$, $E(X^2)=8.5$, and $(EX)^2=6.25$, so the convex square gives $8.5\ge 6.25$. $E(\log X)=\log(4)/2\approx 0.69315$, while $\log(EX)=\log(2.5)\approx 0.91629$, so concavity of log reverses the inequality. Both are strict because X is nonconstant and each function has strict curvature over the support.

title: When Jensen's inequality is equality
body: Can Jensen's inequality be equality when X is nonconstant? Give an explicit convex function and explain why.
answer: Yes. An affine function such as phi(x)=2x+1 is convex, and E[phi(X)]=2EX+1=phi(EX) for every integrable X. Strict inequality for nonconstant X requires strict convexity on its support.

title: A failed Jensen application
body: Someone applies $E(\log X)\le\log(EX)$ to a random variable that equals zero with positive probability. What is wrong with the calculation?
answer: The real logarithm is undefined at zero, and a finite $E(\log X)$ is unavailable. Jensen's finite-expectation form requires the function to be defined on the support and the transformed expectation to exist.

title: Fixed weights during the M step
body: When maximizing Q(Psi;Psi_old) for a mixture, are the responsibilities recomputed for each candidate Psi? Explain.
answer: No. The E step computed responsibilities using Psi_old; they stay fixed while the M step varies candidate Psi. The next E step recomputes them after the parameter update.

title: Zero effective component count
body: A mixture component has effective count N_h=0 after the E step. What fails in the usual weighted-mean M-step update?
answer: Its denominator is zero, so the mean is undefined by that formula. A fitting procedure must handle the boundary or alter initialization or constraints.

title: Two-point mixture M step
body: For x=(0,2), the component-one E-step responsibilities are (0.75,0.25). Find both updated weights and both updated means, with variances fixed.
answer: Effective counts are 1 and 1, so weights are 0.5 and 0.5. The weighted means are 0.5 for component one and 1.5 for component two.

title: One weight-decay update
body: For one weight w=4, current loss gradient 6, learning rate 0.1 and L2 penalty strength 0.2, calculate the ordinary penalized gradient step. Compare it with the unpenalized step.
answer: The penalized gradient is 6+0.2(4)=6.8, so w_new=4-0.1(6.8)=3.32. Equivalently, 0.98(4)-0.1(6)=3.32. Without the penalty the step gives 3.4.

title: Feature units and weight penalties
body: An input is multiplied by ten and its linear-model weight divided by ten, leaving predictions identical. By what factor does that weight's squared penalty contribution change?
answer: It is divided by 100, because (w/10)^2=w^2/100. A raw squared-weight penalty depends on predictor units even when fitted predictions are unchanged.

title: Coupled penalty versus separate decay
body: Why can adding an L2 penalty to a loss produce a different update from a separate weight-decay step under Adam, although they can coincide for ordinary SGD?
answer: An L2 penalty contributes $\lambda$ times the weight to the gradient, so Adam's adaptive coordinate scaling also acts on the penalty gradient. A separate decay step scales the weight directly outside the adaptive gradient calculation. Ordinary scalar-step SGD gives the same algebra after matching the coefficients.

title: The predictable piece of a Wold decomposition
body: A weakly stationary series is written as a linearly predictable series plus a moving average of uncorrelated innovations. What is special about the predictable piece?
answer: Its future values are linear functions of its past, so the innovation variance attached to that piece is zero. That piece is the singular component determined by the linear past. The moving-average piece carries the new unpredictable variation.

title: A conditional probability on a path
body: For discrete variables $X_1,X_2,X_3$ on the pairwise Markov path $1-2-3$, assume $P(X_2=1,X_3=0)>0$. Does $P(X_1=1\mid X_2=1,X_3=0)$ depend on the value $0$ assigned to $X_3$?
answer: No. Conditional independence of the endpoints given the middle variable means the conditional distribution of $X_1$ given $X_2$ and $X_3$ is the conditional distribution of $X_1$ given $X_2$ alone.

title: Why a zero-probability configuration matters
body: The Hammersley–Clifford theorem derives clique factorisation from the pairwise Markov property for a strictly positive density. If some configurations have probability zero, is the converse still guaranteed, and which direction remains valid?
answer: No general converse is guaranteed without positivity: support restrictions can satisfy pairwise conditional independences without a clique factorisation. A proof that takes logarithms of the density or divides by conditional probabilities cannot apply at its zeros. Factorisation still implies the global, and hence pairwise, Markov property wherever the conditional probabilities are defined.

title: Mean number of trials until the first success
body: Independent trials succeed with probability $1/4$. Let $X$ be the trial number of the first success. Find $\mathrm{E}(X)$.
answer: On the trial-count convention, $\mathrm{E}(X)=1/p=4$. The failure-count mean would be $(1-p)/p=3$, one less.

title: A geometric wait that forgets its past
body: Independent Bernoulli trials succeed with probability $1/4$. If $X$ is the trial number of the first success, find $P(X>5\mid X>2)$.
answer: The lack of memory gives $P(X>5\mid X>2)=P(X>3)=(3/4)^3=27/64$.

title: The Conway–Maxwell–Poisson law at unit dispersion
body: The Conway–Maxwell–Poisson probabilities satisfy $P(X=k)/P(X=k-1)=\lambda/k^{\nu}$. What familiar law appears when $\nu=1$?
answer: The ratios become $\lambda/k$, which are the Poisson ratios, and the normalising series is $e^{\lambda}$. The distribution is Poisson with mean $\lambda$.

title: A dispersion parameter above one
body: For $\lambda>0$, compare the successive-probability ratios of a Conway–Maxwell–Poisson law with $\nu=2$ and a Poisson law with mean $\lambda$. Which ratio is smaller for $k>1$, and what does this imply once the probabilities are decreasing in the upper tail?
answer: The ratios are $\lambda/k^2$ and $\lambda/k$, respectively. The first is smaller for every $k>1$. Once both sequences are decreasing, each successive Conway–Maxwell–Poisson probability is a smaller fraction of its predecessor. This compares decay ratios; it does not assert that every individual probability is smaller, since each law must sum to one.

title: Unequal variances and the pooled t statistic
body: Two independent normal samples have unknown means and unknown variances that need not be equal. Is the usual pooled two-sample $t$ statistic exactly Student $t$ when the means are equal?
answer: No. Exact Student calibration of the pooled statistic uses one common variance. When the variances differ, the null distribution depends on the variance ratio and is not a single $t$ law.

title: A Welch standard error
body: Two samples of size $10$ have sample variances $1$ and $4$. The estimated difference of means is $0$. Find the Welch standard error of the difference of means.
answer: The estimated variance of the difference is $1/10+4/10=1/2$, so the standard error is $\sqrt{1/2}$.

title: With $\varepsilon=0.1$, what is $\alpha$, to three decimals?
body: In binary AdaBoost with labels in $\{-1,+1\}$, use $\alpha=\tfrac12\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$ for weighted error $\varepsilon$. With $\varepsilon=0.1$, what is $\alpha$, to three decimals?
answer: $\alpha=\frac12\log(0.9/0.1)=\frac12\log 9\approx 1.099$. The vote is larger than the vote $0.549$ at $\varepsilon=1/4$, because the weak rule is more accurate.

title: A perfect classification round
body: In binary AdaBoost the vote coefficient is $\alpha=\tfrac12\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, where $\varepsilon$ is the weighted classification error. Why is this formula not a finite coefficient when a round classifies every case correctly?
answer: The ratio $(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$ divides by zero, so $\alpha$ is infinite. A weak rule that already classifies every weighted case correctly needs a stopping rule rather than this coefficient.

title: One pair
body: How many pairs do $3$ items make, and how many do $6$ items make?
answer: $\binom32=3$ and $\binom62=15$, since an unordered pair is counted twice among the ordered pairs of distinct items.

title: A zero in the denominator
body: Two partitions of $n\ge2$ objects both put every object in a singleton group. Let $I$ count pairs grouped together in both partitions, and let $A$ and $B$ count pairs grouped together in each partition. What is $I$, and why is the adjusted Rand formula $[I-AB/\binom n2]/[(A+B)/2-AB/\binom n2]$ undefined without a convention for this case?
answer: No pair is together in either partition, so $I=0$ and both pair totals are $0$. The expectation and the ceiling are $0$, and the correction divides by zero. There are no together-pairs whose chance agreement one could subtract.

title: Another shift
body: Start from $3,5,7$ and add $10$ to each observation. Write the centred vector.
answer: The observations are $13,15,17$, the mean is $15$, and the centred vector is again $(-2,0,2)$. The location moved. The ancillary statistic did not.

title: A scale that remains
body: The errors are multiplied by $2$ before the mean is subtracted. What happens to the centred values of $3,5,7$ if those observations are multiplied by $2$?
answer: The observations become $6,10,14$, the mean is $10$, and the centred vector is $(-4,0,4)$, twice $(-2,0,2)$. The centred vector saw the scale. It is not ancillary for a parameter that includes that scale.

title: Which ARIMA orders, and what constant, give a random walk with drift $c$?
body: Which ARIMA orders, and what constant, give a random walk with drift $c$?
answer: The differences have mean $c$ and no further autoregressive or moving-average terms, so the model is ARIMA$(0,1,0)$ with constant $c$.

title: Observations lost by second differencing
body: Second differences of a series satisfy $y''_t=y_t-2y_{t-1}+y_{t-2}$. How many observations are lost relative to the original length $T$?
answer: Each difference drops one time point, so two differences leave $T-2$ values. In practice it is rarely useful to difference more than twice.

title: If every score increases by $\log 2$, do the probabilities change?
body: A baseline-category logit model uses $p_k=e^{\eta_k}/\sum_j e^{\eta_j}$. If every score $\eta_j$, including the reference score, increases by $\log 2$, do the probabilities change?
answer: No. Every exponential is multiplied by $2$, and the factor cancels in the ratio. The reference score is no longer zero, which is why a fit sets one score back to zero without changing the probabilities.

title: Odds between non-reference categories
body: A three-category logit model has scores $\eta_0=0$, $\eta_1=0.5$ and $\eta_2=1$, with $p_k=e^{\eta_k}/\sum_{j=0}^2 e^{\eta_j}$. What is $p_2/p_1$?
answer: The exact probabilities satisfy $p_2/p_1=e^{0.5}\approx 1.6487$. It is the odds of category $2$ against category $1$, not against the reference. The four-decimal probabilities $0.5065$ and $0.3072$ are each rounded, so their ratio is not a second calculation of $e^{0.5}$.

title: How many free linear predictors does a four-category model have?
body: How many free linear predictors does a four-category model have?
answer: Three. One category is the reference and its score is fixed at zero. Four free score vectors would describe the same probabilities more than once.

title: A $p$-value equal to its threshold
body: For $m=5$ and $q^*=0.05$, the third threshold is $0.03$. If the ordered $p$-values are $0.001$, $0.012$, $0.030$, $0.20$, $0.40$, what is $k$ under the closed rule $P_{(i)}\le (i/m)q^*$, and what is $k$ under the strict rule $P_{(j)}<\alpha j/m$?
answer: The closed rule has $0.030\le 0.030$, and $0.20>0.04$, so $k=3$. The strict rule has $0.030<0.030$ false and $0.012<0.020$ true, so its largest index is $2$. Equality is the case in which the two cutoffs separate.

title: Nothing rejected
body: Ordered $p$-values $0.04$, $0.20$, $0.30$, $0.40$, $0.50$ are tested at $m=5$ and $q^*=0.05$. What is rejected?
answer: The first threshold is $0.01$, and $0.04>0.01$. No later comparison can create an earlier success once the largest successful index is sought, and none succeeds, so nothing is rejected.

title: If $T$ is unbiased for $\theta$ and $c$ is a constant, what is the bias of $cT$ for $\theta$?
body: If $T$ is unbiased for $\theta$ and $c$ is a constant, what is the bias of $cT$ for $\theta$?
answer: $\mathbb{E}(cT)=c\theta$, so the bias is $c\theta-\theta=(c-1)\theta$. The choice $c=(n-1)/n$ is the step from $s^2$ to $S_n^2$ when both estimate $\sigma^2$, and it produces bias $-\sigma^2/n$.

title: An estimator has variance $0.3$ and bias $0.1$.
body: An estimator has variance $0.3$ and bias $0.1$. What is its mean squared error?
answer: The mean squared error is $0.3+0.1^2=0.31$. The squared bias is a tenth of the variance, so most of the error is scatter.

title: A zero coefficient
body: A log-linear mean satisfies $\log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1 z$, where $z$ is an indicator. If $\beta_1=0$, what is the ratio of the means at $z=1$ and $z=0$?
answer: $e^{0}=1$. The indicator does not change the fitted mean.

title: The other side of the bend
body: The quadratic $-0.0076\,s^2+0.1793\,s$ at $s=0$ is $0$. At the turning point the added log-mean is about $1.0575$. Is the fitted size curve higher at $s=11.80$ than at $s=0$?
answer: Yes. The factor $2.879$ is greater than $1$, and the square term is negative, so this is a maximum rather than a minimum. Past the turning point the quadratic pulls the log-mean back down.

title: Four raw $p$-values
body: Which of $0.02$ and $0.01$ are rejected by a four-test Bonferroni rule at family-wise level $0.05$?
answer: The adjusted values are $0.08$ and $0.04$. Only $0.01$, with adjusted value $0.04$, is rejected.

title: The independent calculation
body: For four independent tests at level $0.0125$, is the family-wise error equal to $0.05$?
answer: No. It equals $1-(0.9875)^4\approx 0.0491$, which is less than $0.05$. The value $0.05$ is the union bound, not the independent probability.

title: Six tests
body: A raw $p$-value is $0.01$ and there are six tests. What is the Bonferroni adjusted value at family-wise level $0.05$, and is it rejected?
answer: The adjusted value is $0.06$, which is greater than $0.05$, so the null is not rejected. The per-test level would have been $0.05/6\approx 0.00833$, and $0.01$ is larger than that level.

title: A round with $\varepsilon=0.4$ still has a positive vote.
body: Binary AdaBoost uses $\alpha=\tfrac12\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$ and multiplies a case weight by $e^{-\alpha y h(x)}$, where $y,h(x)\in\{-1,+1\}$. For weighted error $\varepsilon=0.4$, find $\alpha$ to four decimals and the ratio of the incorrect-case multiplier to the correct-case multiplier.
answer: $\alpha=\frac12\log(0.6/0.4)=\frac12\log 1.5\approx 0.2027$. The relative factor is $0.6/0.4=1.5$.

title: Two stumps vote $+1$ and $-1$ with coefficients $0.6$ and $0.2$.
body: Two stumps vote $+1$ and $-1$ with coefficients $0.6$ and $0.2$. What sign does the ensemble return?
answer: The weighted vote is $0.6-0.2=0.4>0$, so the ensemble returns $+1$.

title: After one step
body: A time-homogeneous Markov chain on states $1,2$ has transition matrix $P=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.2\\0.4&0.6\end{pmatrix}$, with row $i$ giving the next-state probabilities from $i$. Starting at $X_0=1$, find $\mathbb P(X_1=1)$ and $\mathbb P(X_2=1)$.
answer: $\mathbb{P}(X_1=1)=0.8$, the $(1,1)$ entry of $P$. $\mathbb{P}(X_2=1)=0.72$, the $(1,1)$ entry of $P^2$. The one-step probability is not the two-step probability.

title: A route of length three
answer: Condition on the state at time $2$: $0.72\times 0.8+0.28\times 0.4=0.576+0.112=0.688$. This is the $(1,1)$ entry of $P^2 P$, which Chapman–Kolmogorov identifies with $P^3$.

title: Degrees of freedom
body: How many degrees of freedom does the Pearson chi-squared test of independence use for a $3\times4$ contingency table with no structural zeros?

title: A cell below the warning line
body: One fitted count is $3.2$ and the others exceed $5$. What does the small-cell condition say about the chi-squared approximation?
answer: The approximation is unreliable when an estimated frequency is small, and the stated threshold is less than $5$. A fitted count of $3.2$ falls under that warning. Combining categories is the remedy only when the combined categories still make sense.

title: In the matrix with rows $(0,1)$ and $(0,1)$, is $\{0,1\}$ a communicating class?
body: In the matrix with rows $(0,1)$ and $(0,1)$, is $\{0,1\}$ a communicating class?
answer: No. State $1$ does not lead to state $0$, so the states do not communicate. There are two classes, $\{0\}$ and $\{1\}$.

title: For the alternation, does $\pi=(1/2,1/2)$ satisfy $\pi P=\pi$?
body: A Markov chain on states $1,2$ alternates deterministically, with transition matrix $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Does $\pi=(1/2,1/2)$ satisfy $\pi P=\pi$? Does that imply that $P^n$ converges?
answer: Yes. Each coordinate of $\pi P$ is $1/2$, because each column of $P$ contains a single $1$. The chain still has period $2$, so the stationary equation has a solution and $P^n$ does not converge.

title: If a state has a self-loop, what is its period?
body: If a state has a self-loop, what is its period?
answer: The period is $1$. A return in one step is on the list whose greatest common divisor is the period, and that divisor is then $1$. The rest of the class is aperiodic as well.

title: An all-zero exponent
body: A case in a two-component mixture has known label $1$, encoded by $(z_1,z_2)=(1,0)$. Its likelihood contribution is $(\pi_1 f_1(x))^{z_1}(\pi_2 f_2(x))^{z_2}$, where both weighted densities are positive. Why does the component-$2$ factor equal $1$ rather than $0$?
answer: The exponent is the indicator that the case came from component $2$. It is $0$, and a positive number to the power $0$ is $1$. The factor drops out of the product. It is not a probability of zero.

title: Observed versus complete
body: At an observation $x$, a two-component mixture has weights $\pi_1=0.4$, $\pi_2=0.6$ and densities $f_1(x)=0.5$, $f_2(x)=0.1$. Compare its complete-data contribution when the label is $1$ with its observed-data contribution when the label is unobserved. Which is larger, and why?
answer: The observed contribution $0.26$ is larger. It equals $0.2+0.06$, the sum of the two possible complete contributions.

title: In the unbalanced table, recovery under A is $4/5$ for men and $2/5$ for women.
body: Among patients receiving treatment A, $8$ of $10$ men and $40$ of $100$ women recover. Is the pooled recovery rate a weighted average of the two within-sex rates, and what are the weights?
answer:
Yes. The weights are the sex counts in A, $10/110$ and $100/110$:

$$
\frac{10}{110}\cdot\frac{4}{5}+\frac{100}{110}\cdot\frac{2}{5}=\frac{48}{110}.
$$


The weights are not $1/2$ and $1/2$.

title: Men recover at $7/10$ under B and women at $3/10$.
body: Men recover at $7/10$ under B and women at $3/10$. If B's patients were half men and half women, what recovery rate would the same within-sex rates give?
answer: $\frac12\cdot 7/10+\frac12\cdot 3/10=1/2$. That is the balanced figure already computed for B, not the pooled $73/110$ from the unbalanced table.

title: A total of twelve
body: Two independent fair dice. Find $\Pr(X+Y=12)$.
answer: Only $(6,6)$ works, so the probability is $1/36$. The convolution has a single term.

title: Dependent uniforms are a different integral
body: If $X$ is uniform on $[0,1]$ and $Y=X$, what is wrong with writing the sum's density as the convolution of the two marginal uniforms?
answer: $X$ and $Y$ are not independent, and $X+Y=2X$ is supported on $[0,2]$ with a different law from the triangular convolution. The product $f_X(x)f_Y(z-x)$ is the joint density only under independence. The dependent calculation uses the joint distribution along $y=x$.

title: The empty event
body: Use countable additivity for a probability measure to show that $P(\emptyset)=0$. Which disjoint sequence of sets can be used?
answer: $P(\emptyset)=0$. The sequence is $\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots$, a disjoint sequence whose union is $\emptyset$, so the probability equals the sum of infinitely many copies of itself.

title: Two events, then nothing
body: Let $A$ and $B$ be disjoint with $P(A)=P(B)=1/4$, and set every later set empty. What is $P(A\cup B)$?
answer: Countable additivity gives $1/4+1/4+0+0+\cdots=1/2$. Finite additivity is this axiom with the tail sets empty.

title: A Poisson mean
body: For $n$ independent Poisson($\lambda$) observations, $\mathcal{I}(\lambda)=n/\lambda$. What is the bound for an unbiased estimator of $\lambda$, and does $\overline X$ meet it?
answer: A single Poisson log probability $-\lambda+X\log\lambda$ has score $X/\lambda-1$, with variance $\operatorname{Var}(X)/\lambda^2=1/\lambda$. For $n$ independent copies, $\mathcal{I}(\lambda)=n/\lambda$, and the bound is $\lambda/n$. The sample mean is unbiased with that variance, so it meets the bound.

title: A target with derivative zero
body: In a regular one-parameter model with finite positive Fisher information $\mathcal I(\theta)$, the Cramér–Rao bound for an unbiased estimator of $g(\theta)$ is $[g'(\theta)]^2/\mathcal I(\theta)$. If $g'(\theta_0)=0$, what does the bound say at $\theta_0$?
answer: The numerator is zero, so the bound is $0$. That does not by itself produce an estimator with variance zero. It says the inequality gives no positive floor at a stationary point of $g$.

title: On the four-point dendrogram, how many clusters does a cut at height $0.5$ return, and how many does a cut at height $7$ return?
body: Four points at $0$, $1$, $4$ and $10$ are clustered by single linkage using absolute differences. How many clusters does a horizontal cut at height $0.5$ return, and how many does a cut at height $7$ return?
answer: Height $0.5$ is below every merge, so there are four clusters, the four points. Height $7$ is above the last merge at $6$, so there is one cluster.

title: Why is the single-linkage distance from $\{0,1\}$ to $4$ equal to $3$ rather than $4$?
body: Why is the single-linkage distance from $\{0,1\}$ to $4$ equal to $3$ rather than $4$?
answer: Single linkage takes the closest pair across the two groups. That pair is $1$ and $4$, at distance $3$. The distance $4$ is the complete-linkage height, using $0$ and $4$.

title: Both rows of a two-state matrix equal $(1/2,1/2)$.
body: Both rows of a two-state matrix equal $(1/2,1/2)$. What is the two-step probability of moving from state $1$ to state $2$?
answer: Every one-step probability into state $2$ is $1/2$, so the two-step probability is $(1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/2)=1/2$. The square of this matrix equals the matrix itself.

title: Successive states of a Markov chain are not automatically independent.
body: A Markov chain on states $1,2$ has transition matrix $P=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.2\\0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}$. Why is the next state more likely to be $2$ after state $2$ than after state $1$? What does this show about dependence between successive states when both current states have positive probability?
answer: The second row puts probability $0.5$ on staying in state $2$, while the first row puts only $0.2$ there. Different rows mean the next state still carries information about the current state.

title: A monotone validation curve
body: Validation errors after epochs $1$ through $5$ are $0.40$, $0.33$, $0.29$, $0.27$, $0.26$. A stopping rule stops at the first increase in validation error and retains the epoch with lowest validation error. Has it stopped by epoch $5$, and which epoch is best so far?
answer: The rule has not stopped, because validation error has decreased at each observed epoch. The fifth epoch is best so far, with error $0.26$. This does not imply that a later epoch will be worse; it only identifies the best of the five completed epochs.

title: Training versus validation
body: At epoch $4$ the training error is $0.14$ and the validation error is $0.29$. At epoch $3$ the training error is $0.21$ and the validation error is $0.27$. Which epoch does early stopping keep?
answer: Epoch $3$, because $0.27<0.29$. The lower training error at epoch $4$ is the quantity the rule is refusing to chase.

title: Batch versus online
body: A training set has $5000$ cases. How many online updates equal one epoch, and how many batch updates equal one epoch?
answer: Online learning updates after every case, so one epoch is $5000$ updates. Batch learning updates once from the full sum, so one epoch is $1$ update.

title: A remainder
body: A training set contains $n=20$ cases and is traversed in non-overlapping mini-batches of size $m=4$, once per epoch. After $7$ parameter updates, how many full epochs and how many batches of the next epoch have been completed?
answer: Five updates finish the first epoch. The next two updates are two of the five batches of the second epoch. The run has completed $1$ epoch and $2/5$ of the next, which is $7/5=1.4$ epochs.

title: Offspring probabilities $p_0=1/8$, $p_1=1/8$, $p_2=3/4$.
body: Offspring probabilities $p_0=1/8$, $p_1=1/8$, $p_2=3/4$. Is the mean above $1$?
answer: The mean is $1/8+2\cdot 3/4=1/8+3/2=13/8>1$. Extinction is not certain. The probability itself is the smaller root of $f(s)=s$, not the mean.

title: If $p_0=0$ and $p_2=1$, what is the extinction probability, and what is the mean?
body: If $p_0=0$ and $p_2=1$, what is the extinction probability, and what is the mean?
answer: Every individual has two children, so the mean is $2$ and generation $n$ has size $2^n$. The process never hits $0$, and the extinction probability is $0$. The root $s=0$ of $f(s)=s^2$ is that probability.

title: A larger exponential sample
body: Compute $(1-1/50)^{50}$ and say whether it is closer to $e^{-1}=0.36788$ than $(1-1/20)^{20}=0.35849$ is.
answer: $(1-1/50)^{50}=0.36417$. The gap to $0.36788$ is $0.00371$, smaller than the gap $0.00939$ at $n=20$. The limit statement is visible in the arithmetic.

title: Which type has a finite upper end?
body: Let $M_n$ be the maximum of $n$ independent $\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$ observations. Which extreme-value type describes the limit of $n(M_n-1)$? Equivalently, what nonnegative limit does $n(1-M_n)$ have, and why is this not a Gumbel limit?
answer: For $x\ge0$ and $n>x$, $P(n(1-M_n)>x)=(1-x/n)^n\to e^{-x}$. Thus the gap converges to an exponential law of rate $1$, and its negative has the reversed Weibull extreme-value law with shape $1$. It has a finite upper endpoint at zero, whereas the Gumbel law has support on the whole real line.

title: Sorted $p$-values $0.01$ and $0.04$, with $M=2$ and level $0.05$.
body: Two hypotheses have sorted $p$-values $0.01$ and $0.04$. Apply the Benjamini–Hochberg step-up rule at level $0.05$. How many hypotheses are rejected?
answer: The thresholds are $0.025$ and $0.05$. Then $0.01<0.025$ and $0.04<0.05$, so both are rejected.

title: In that two-test rejection, could the realised false-discovery proportion still be $1$?
body: The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure rejects both hypotheses in a two-test family at level $0.05$. Could the realised false-discovery proportion still equal $1$? Explain the distinction between the realised proportion and its expectation.
answer: Yes. If both nulls are true, then $V=R=2$ and the proportion is $1$. Control of the expected proportion does not cap the proportion on a single list.

title: Row sums
body: A continuous-time Markov chain alternates between idle and busy, leaving idle at rate $2$ per hour and busy at rate $4$ per hour. Write its generator, in that state order, and find both row sums.
answer: Each row sums to $0$: $-2+2=0$ and $4-4=0$.

title: Time versus visits
body: A continuous-time Markov chain alternates between idle and busy, leaving idle at rate $2$ per hour and busy at rate $4$ per hour. In the long run, what fraction of visits does the jump chain spend idle, and what fraction of time does the continuous-time chain spend idle?
answer: The jump chain alternates, so half of the visits are idle. The time average is $2/3$, because idle spells last twice as long as busy spells.

title: One hour
body: A continuous-time Markov chain leaves idle at rate $2$ per hour and busy at rate $4$ per hour. Starting idle, what is the probability of being busy after one hour, to four decimals, and what stationary probability does it approach?
answer: The probability is $(1-e^{-6})/3\approx 0.3325$. The stationary probability of busy is $1/3\approx 0.3333$.

title: A pure node
body: All $10$ cases in a node belong to one class. What is the Gini index?
answer: One proportion is $1$ and the others are $0$, so $1-\sum\hat p_g^2=0$. Two draws from the node always match.

title: The even two-class node
body: For two classes with $p=1/2$, what is $2p(1-p)$?
answer: $2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac12$. This is the largest two-class value: the quadratic $2p(1-p)$ opens downwards and its vertex is at $p=1/2$.

title: A diagonal feature map
body: Two inputs map to $\phi(x_1)=(2,0)$ and $\phi(x_2)=(0,3)$. Write the Gram matrix and its eigenvalues.
answer: The products are $4$, $0$ and $9$, so $K_S=\operatorname{diag}(4,9)$. The eigenvalues are $4$ and $9$. The off-diagonal zeros record orthogonal features.

title: A coefficient that cancels
body: The feature vectors $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ have Gram matrix $K_S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$. For $c=(1,1,-1)^\top$, compute $c^\top K_Sc$ and explain what it implies about these feature vectors.
answer:
$$
c^\top K_S c=\bigl\|(1,0)+(0,1)-(1,1)\bigr\|^2=\|(0,0)\|^2=0.
$$


The three feature vectors with these coefficients sum to the zero vector, so the quadratic form contributes nothing even though $c$ itself is not zero.

title: A keen reverse jump
body: Using $p(1)=0.2$, $p(3)=0.5$, $J(1\mid 3)=0.4$ and $J(3\mid 1)=0.1$, find $r$ for a move from $1$ to $3$.
answer:
$$
r=\frac{0.5\times 0.4}{0.2\times 0.1}=10.
$$
The acceptance probability is $1$. The proposal rarely offers the move, and the target density is higher at the destination, so the correction makes the ratio larger than $1$.

title: Where the correction is idle
body: A proposal adds an increment drawn from $N(0,1)$, independent of the sign. What is the Hastings correction?
answer: The increment density is symmetric, so $J(\omega+d\mid\omega)=J(\omega\mid\omega+d)$. The correction equals $1$ and the acceptance ratio reduces to the ratio of target densities.

title: How many distinct heights?
body: For four clinics and three merges, what is the largest number of distinct cophenetic values the dendrogram can contain, and how many pairs are there?
answer: There are $6$ pairs and at most $3$ distinct cophenetic values, one per merge. In the average-linkage tree the distinct values are $1$, $2$, and $10.5$.

title: Complete-linkage average
body: The six cophenetic values under complete linkage are $1$, $2$, and four copies of $12$. What is their average?

title: A cut
body: Four points at $0$, $1$, $10$ and $12$ are clustered by average linkage with absolute differences. Does a horizontal cut at height $6$ return two clusters or one?
answer: Height $6$ lies between $2$ and $10.5$, so the two pairs have been formed and have not yet been joined. The cut returns two clusters.

title: What is the hinge at margin $0.2$, and what is the slope of the hinge, as a function of the margin, just to the left of $1$?
body: What is the hinge at margin $0.2$, and what is the slope of the hinge, as a function of the margin, just to the left of $1$?
answer: The hinge is $1-0.2=0.8$. Just to the left of $1$ the slope in the margin is $-1$.

title: The contribution of the ridge penalty
body: A support-vector criterion is $\sum_i[1-y_i f(x_i)]_++(\lambda/2)\lVert\beta\rVert^2$. With total hinge loss $2.25$, $\lambda=2$ and $\lVert\beta\rVert=1$, what is the criterion value?
answer: The penalty is $(2/2)(1)=1$. The criterion value is $2.25+1=3.25$. A larger $\lambda$ charges the same weight more heavily and tolerates more hinge.

title: The remaining holding time
body: A holding time is exponential with constant rate $2$ per hour. Conditional on already having waited $1$ hour without a transition, what is the probability of waiting at least one further hour?
answer: Memorylessness makes the remaining wait a fresh exponential of rate $2$, so the probability is $e^{-2}\approx 0.1353$. The hour already spent does not appear in the answer.

title: Exit rates $3$ and $1$ leave a state.
body: Exit rates $3$ and $1$ leave a state. What is the probability that the rate-$3$ clock rings first, and what is the mean hold?
answer: The total rate is $4$, so the rate-$3$ clock wins with probability $3/4=0.75$. The mean hold is $1/4=0.25$ time unit.

title: For $n=6$, $p=2$, mean $(1,1)$ and $S=2I_2$, what is the transformed statistic?
body: A sample of size $n=6$ in $p=2$ dimensions has mean $(1,1)^\top$ and sample covariance $S=2I_2$. To test a zero population mean, find $T^2=n\bar x^\top S^{-1}\bar x$ and its transformed statistic $(n-p)T^2/[p(n-1)]$.
answer: $2.4$. Here $T^2=6$ and the factor is $4/10=0.4$.

title: A statistic against an F quantile
body: Does $2.4$ exceed the $0.95$ quantile of $F_{2,4}$?
answer: No. That quantile is $6.944$. The upper tail probability of $2.4$ is $0.2066$.

title: When $p=1$, $n=5$, $\bar x=2$ and $s=1$, what is $T^2$?
body: For the one-dimensional test of a zero mean, let $n=5$, $\bar x=2$ and sample standard deviation $s=1$. What is Hotelling's $T^2=n\bar x^2/s^2$?
answer: $20$, which equals $t^2$. The $F$ factor is $1$ in this one-dimensional case, so the transformed statistic is also $20$.

title: A zero in the table
body: $\Pr(X=1)=1/2$, $\Pr(Y=1)=1/3$ and $\Pr(X=1,Y=1)=0$. Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?
answer: No. The product of the marginals is $1/6$, and the joint probability is $0$. One cell where the product formula fails is enough.

title: A fair pair of coins
body: Two independent fair coins. Find $\Pr(\text{both heads})$ and $\E[XY]$ if a head is coded $1$ and a tail $0$.
answer: Each head has probability $1/2$, so both heads have probability $1/4$. That event is $\{XY=1\}$, and $XY$ is $0$ otherwise, so $\E[XY]=1/4$. This equals $\E[X]\E[Y]=(1/2)\times(1/2)$.

title: An absorbing state
body: All rates out of state $0$ are $0$. What is the jump chain's behaviour at $0$?
answer: $\nu_0=0$, so there is no next state. The holding time is infinite and the jump chain stays at $0$.

title: Two equal rates
body: A continuous-time Markov chain can leave state $1$ only for states $2$ and $3$, with rates $q_{12}=q_{13}=5$ per hour. Find the two jump probabilities and the mean holding time in state $1$.
answer: $\nu_1=10$, so each destination has probability $5/10=1/2$. The mean holding time is $1/10$.

title: A zero that should be zero
body: Compute $D(p\,\Vert\,p)$ for $p=(0.8,0.2)$.
answer: Each ratio is $1$, and $\log 1=0$, so the divergence is $0$.

title: Which direction is larger?
answer: $D(q\,\Vert\,p)\approx 0.2231$ nats. The smaller number $0.1927$ is $D(p\,\Vert\,q)$, the penalty for using a fair coin when the truth is $p$.

title: Bits
body: For $p=(0.8,0.2)$ and $q=(0.5,0.5)$, calculate $D(p\Vert q)=\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/q_i)$ in nats. Divide the unrounded value by $\log 2$ and report the divergence in bits to four decimals.
answer: The unrounded divergence divided by $\log 2$ equals $0.2781$ bits.

title: The multiplier
body: Gradient descent on $E(w)=(w-3)^2$ uses $w_{r+1}=w_r-\varepsilon E'(w_r)$. Which constant learning rates $\varepsilon$ strictly decrease the loss at every step with $w_r\ne3$?
answer: Those with $0<\varepsilon<1$. The absolute value of $1-2\varepsilon$ is then below $1$. At $\varepsilon=1$ the error keeps its size and changes sign.

title: Two steps from 5
body: Gradient descent on $E(w)=(w-3)^2$ uses $w_{r+1}=w_r-\varepsilon E'(w_r)$. Starting at $w_0=5$ with $\varepsilon=0.4$, find the next two weights.
answer: The multiplier is $0.2$. The error $2$ becomes $0.4$, so the first weight is $3.4$. The error $0.4$ becomes $0.08$, so the second weight is $3.08$.

title: A finite sum of steps
body: Why can a positive learning-rate sequence $\gamma_r=1/r^2$ provide insufficient total movement in gradient descent, whereas $\gamma_r=1/r$ satisfies the usual divergent-sum requirement? Does this requirement alone guarantee convergence?
answer: The sum $\sum_{r=1}^\infty1/r^2$ is finite, whereas $\sum_{r=1}^\infty1/r$ diverges. If the gradient is bounded, a finite total step size can leave a positive distance to the minimiser. Divergence of the step-size sum prevents this particular obstruction, but convergence also depends on the objective, gradient noise and other step-size conditions.

title: For $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$, $(2,4)$, what is the fitted height at $x=1$?
body: For $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$, $(2,4)$, what is the fitted height at $x=1$?
answer: $2$, the mean of $y$. The arithmetic is $0.5+1.5\cdot 1=2$.

title: Constraining the intercept to zero
body: For observations $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$ and $(2,4)$, find the least-squares slope when the fitted line is constrained to pass through the origin.
answer: $9/5=1.8$. The products $x_i y_i$ sum to $9$ and the squares $x_i^2$ sum to $5$.

title: Why is the origin line's residual sum of squares $1.8$ rather than $1.5$?
body: For observations $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$ and $(2,4)$, explain why the least-squares residual sum of squares is $1.8$ when the intercept is fixed at zero and $1.5$ when an intercept is fitted.
answer: The origin line is not allowed an intercept. The free line reaches $1.5$ by using intercept $0.5$. Inside the origin-only family, $1.8$ is the minimum.

title: The hundred tosses
body: For $100$ fair tosses, what are the exact probability $\mathrm{P}(S\ge 60)$, the plain normal approximation, and the continuity-corrected approximation, to four decimals?
answer: The exact value is $0.0284$. The plain approximation is $0.0228$. The continuity correction is $0.0287$.

title: Chebyshev against the normal tail
body: Let $S\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(100,1/2)$. The Chebyshev bound on $P(|S/100-1/2|\ge0.1)$ is $0.25$, while the uncorrected normal approximation to $P(S\ge60)$ is about $0.023$. Why is there no contradiction?
answer: Chebyshev's inequality is an upper bound that uses only the variance. The normal approximation estimates the probability. An upper bound of $0.25$ is compatible with a probability near $0.046$ for the two tails.

title: Twenty tosses
body: For $S\sim\mathrm{Bin}(20,1/2)$, the exact $\mathrm{P}(S\le 8)$ is $0.2517$ and the plain normal value is $0.186$. What does the continuity correction do?
answer: It reads the normal distribution at $8.5$ rather than at $8$, and the value is about $0.251$, close to $0.2517$. The plain reading at $8$ is the one that sits low.

title: A zero predictor
body: Give the identity, log and logit means at $\eta=0$.
answer: The identity mean is $0$. The log-link mean is $e^{0}=1$. The logit mean is $1/2$. Zero is a legal log mean only in the limit $\eta\to-\infty$; at $\eta=0$ the log mean is $1$.

title: A coefficient on the log scale
body: Under a log link, $\eta=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$ and $\beta_1=0.2$. By what factor does the mean change when $x$ increases by $1$?
answer: The mean is multiplied by $e^{0.2}=1.2214$ to four decimals. The identity link would have added $0.2$ instead of multiplying.

title: A server completes $12$ jobs an hour, and the mean number of jobs in the system is $3$.
body: A server completes $12$ jobs an hour, and the mean number of jobs in the system is $3$. What is the mean sojourn, in minutes?
answer: $W=3/12=1/4$ hour, which is $15$ minutes. The completion rate in a stable system is the accepted arrival rate.

title: The mean wait in the queue is $10$ minutes and the mean service is $5$ minutes, with $12$ jobs an hour accepted.
body: The mean wait in the queue is $10$ minutes and the mean service is $5$ minutes, with $12$ jobs an hour accepted. What are $L_q$ and $L$?
answer: Ten minutes is $1/6$ hour and five minutes is $1/12$ hour, so $W=1/6+1/12=1/4$ hour. Then $L_q=12\times 1/6=2$ and $L=12\times 1/4=3$.

title: Variance in the second component
body: The correlation matrix of two standardised variables is $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.8\\0.8&1\end{pmatrix}$. What fraction of the total variance belongs to the second principal component?
answer: The eigenvalues sum to the trace $2$, so the second component accounts for $0.2/2=0.1$.

title: A unit loading of $0.6$ belongs to a component of variance $0.25$.
body: Principal components are calculated from standardised variables of variance $1$. A coordinate of a unit eigenvector is $0.6$, and its eigenvalue is $0.25$. What is the correlation between that variable and the corresponding component score?
answer: The correlation is $0.6\sqrt{0.25}=0.6\times 0.5=0.3$.

title: A stationary probability ratio
body: A birth–death chain on states $0,1,2$ has stationary probabilities $(4/7,2/7,1/7)$. What is $\pi_2/\pi_1$, and which ratio of birth and death rates must it equal under local balance?
answer: $\pi_2/\pi_1=(1/7)/(2/7)=1/2$, and the cut says this equals $\lambda_1/\mu_2=1/2$.

title: Constant rates on an infinite state space
body: A birth–death chain on $\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ has birth rates $\lambda_n=1$ for every $n\ge0$ and death rates $\mu_n=1$ for every $n\ge1$. Can its local-balance product weights be normalised to a stationary probability distribution?
answer: No. Every weight equals $\pi_0$, and $\sum_n 1$ diverges. The equations still define an invariant measure.

title: A zero predictor
body: Give the logit and probit probabilities at $\eta=0$, and the complementary log-log probability to four decimals.
answer: The logit and the probit both equal $1/2$. Complementary log-log equals $1-\exp(-1)=0.6321$ to four decimals. Symmetry about $1/2$ fails at the origin for that link.

title: A large positive predictor
body: As $\eta\to\infty$, what happens to each of the three probabilities?
answer: Each tends to $1$. The logit ratio $e^{\eta}/(1+e^{\eta})$ does, $\Phi(\eta)$ does, and $\exp(-e^{\eta})$ tends to $0$, so complementary log-log tends to $1$. The limits agree; the speed at a finite $\eta$ does not.

title: Reading the graph
body: A Markov random field has path graph $X-Y-Z$. Which pair is conditionally independent given the third variable under the global Markov property, and which pairs are neighbours?
answer: $X$ and $Z$ are the non-adjacent pair, so the pairwise property says $X\perp Z\mid Y$. The edges are $X-Y$ and $Y-Z$. The pairwise property does not say that an adjacent pair is conditionally independent given the remaining variable.

title: A numerical check of the margin
body: Let $Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$. Conditional on $Y=y$, let $X$ and $Z$ be independent Bernoulli variables with success probability $0.8$ if $y=1$ and $0.2$ if $y=0$. Compute $P(X=1,Z=0)$.
answer: Given $Y=1$ the probability is $0.8\times 0.2=0.16$. Given $Y=0$ it is $0.2\times 0.8=0.16$. The marginal is $\tfrac12(0.16)+\tfrac12(0.16)=0.16$.

title: The hour-long job
body: A nonnegative duration has mean $10$ minutes. What does Markov's inequality say about a duration of at least $60$ minutes?
answer: The probability is at most $10/60=1/6$. If the variance is $25$, Chebyshev's inequality further bounds the same event by $25/50^2=0.01$.

title: Equality
body: Construct a nonnegative law with mean $4$ for which $\mathrm{P}(X\ge 20)=0.2$.
answer: Put probability $0.2$ on $20$ and probability $0.8$ on $0$. The mean is $4$ and the tail probability equals $0.2$, so Markov's bound is attained.

title: An exponential tail
body: For an exponential law with mean $10$, compute $e^{-6}$ to six decimals and compare it with $1/6$.
answer: $e^{-6}\approx 0.002479$, while $1/6\approx 0.1667$. Markov's bound is valid and about $67$ times the exponential probability. The exponential number uses the survival formula. The Markov number uses only the mean.

title: One case
body: For an intercept-only predictor $w$, a case with response $y$ has loss $\tfrac12(w-y)^2$. At $w=0$, what is the online gradient for the case $y=7$ from the responses $1,3,5,7$?
answer: The gradient is $0-7=-7$. It is an unbiased draw from the four case gradients $-1,-3,-5,-7$, whose mean is $-4$, but this particular draw is far from $-4$.

title: A deterministic partition
body: For case loss $\tfrac12(w-y)^2$, evaluate the two mean gradients at $w=0$ on batches with responses $\{1,5\}$ and $\{3,7\}$. Why does averaging these gradients give the full-data gradient $-4$, although neither batch was sampled at random?
answer: The two batches partition the sample, so the average of their means is the mean of all four responses. Random sampling is not required for that identity. Unbiasedness of one batch requires the random draw.

title: A constant ratio
body: For the Poisson samples $(2,0,5)$ and $(1,3,3)$, what is the likelihood ratio, and does it depend on $\lambda$?
answer: The ratio is $36/240=0.15$ for every $\lambda>0$. The sums both equal $7$, so the powers of $\lambda$ cancel.

title: A ratio that moves
body: Evaluate $0.1\lambda^3$ at $\lambda=1$ and at $\lambda=2$.
answer: The values are $0.1$ and $0.8$. The ratio of $(2,0,5)$ against $(4,0,0)$ depends on $\lambda$, and the sums $7$ and $4$ differ.

title: A uniform window
body: Observations $0.2$, $0.9$, $1.1$ come from $\mathrm{Uniform}(\theta,\theta+1)$. For which $\theta$ is the likelihood positive?
answer: The parameter must satisfy $\theta\le 0.2$ and $\theta\ge 0.1$, so $\theta$ lies in $[0.1,0.2]$. The range $0.9$ does not determine this interval.

title: Three observed responses are $4$, $4$ and $10$, and one planned response is missing.
body: Three observed responses are $4$, $4$ and $10$, and one planned response is missing. What is the observed mean?
answer: The observed mean is $(4+4+10)/3=6$.

title: Why is inventing a mixture component label a different problem from estimating that missing response?
body: Three planned responses are observed as $4$, $4$ and $10$, while a fourth response is missing. Explain why assigning latent mixture-component labels to the three observed responses is a different problem from estimating the missing response.
answer: The component label was never one of the intended measurements; it is part of a complete-data story. The missing response was a measurement the design meant to record. The two holes are filled by different models.

title: Variance inflation from correlated predictors
body: Two predictor vectors are $x_1=(1,2,3,4,5)$ and $x_2=(2,4,5,8,11)$. Let $r$ be their sample correlation. Compute $1-r^2$ and the associated variance inflation factor.

title: What happens to the least-squares slopes if $x_2=(2,4,6,8,10)$?
body: A least-squares regression includes an intercept and predictors $x_1=(1,2,3,4,5)$ and $x_2=(2,4,6,8,10)$. Are its two slope coefficients uniquely determined? Explain.
answer: $x_2=2x_1$ exactly, the determinant is $0$, and there is no unique slope pair. Any coefficient on $x_1$ can be traded against the coefficient on $x_2$ without changing fitted means.

title: Is the simple slope $0.7$ the partial slope of $x_1$?
